oneLineAnswer: A prescription tablet for adults with chronic myeloid leukemia that blocks the protein driving it.
whatItIs: Asciminib is a prescription cancer medicine sold under the brand name Scemblix. It comes as film-coated tablets that you swallow whole. Only adults are approved to use it. It treats chronic myeloid leukemia, or CML, a cancer of the bone marrow and blood. CML usually moves slowly rather than fast. Asciminib belongs to a group of medicines called kinase inhibitors. These block specific proteins inside cells.
whatItDoes: CML starts when a piece of DNA moves from one chromosome to another. That creates an abnormal gene called BCR-ABL1.
That gene tells the bone marrow to make an abnormal protein, which pushes leukemia cells to keep growing.
Asciminib attaches to a pocket on that protein, called the myristoyl pocket, and shuts its signal down.
It is approved for adults in three situations. These are newly diagnosed CML in chronic phase, CML already treated, and CML with the T315I mutation.

One trial followed 405 people with newly diagnosed CML. At 48 weeks, 68% on asciminib had a major molecular response, against 49% on other targeted drugs. BCR-ABL1 blood tests measure how much of the abnormal gene remains. A major molecular response is one category used to report those results.
howPeopleUseIt: A cancer specialist prescribes it. It is not something you buy or start on your own.
You take it as a tablet by mouth. The label says to take it away from food and to swallow the tablets whole. Do not break or crush them.
In the trials, people kept taking it until the leukemia got worse or side effects became too much.
Treatment is open-ended. People on it have regular blood tests for blood counts and pancreas enzymes. Blood pressure is checked too.

commonSideEffects: Aching in muscles, joints or bones. This was the most frequent complaint, reported by 29% of people on asciminib in one trial.
Colds and similar upper respiratory infections, reported by about 18%.
Loose stools or diarrhea, reported by about 18%.
Blood test changes. These include lower white cell, platelet and red cell counts, and higher pancreas, cholesterol, uric acid and liver values.
seriousSigns: Low blood counts, called myelosuppression. In a pooled group of 556 people, low platelets occurred in 28%. Low neutrophils occurred in 22%. Some cases were severe.
Pancreas problems. Pancreatitis was reported in 2% of that group, and raised pancreas enzymes in 20%. The label asks for monthly checks of those enzymes.
High blood pressure. It occurred in 18%, and was severe in 10%.
Allergic-type reactions, reported in 31%. These included rash, swelling and bronchospasm, which is narrowing of the airways.
Heart and blood vessel problems were reported in 12% of that group. Cardiac failure was reported in 2.3%. Five deaths (0.9%) occurred.
Harm to a fetus if the medicine is taken during pregnancy.
whoShouldAvoid: People who are pregnant or who could become pregnant. The label says the medicine can harm a fetus. It asks for a pregnancy test before starting. Effective contraception is advised during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose.
People who are breastfeeding. The label advises not to breastfeed during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose.
Children. Safety and effectiveness below adult age have not been established.
The label lists no absolute contraindications, so it does not name any group that must never use this medicine.

interactions: CYP3A4 is a liver enzyme that clears many medicines out of the body. Strong blockers of CYP3A4 raise asciminib levels and the chance of side effects.
Itraconazole taken as an oral solution, an antifungal medicine, lowers asciminib levels and should not be combined with it.
Strong CYP3A4 inducers lower asciminib levels, which may make it work less well.
Asciminib also blocks CYP3A4, CYP2C9, P-gp and BCRP. That can raise the levels of other medicines these enzymes and pumps clear.
The label says to avoid combining asciminib with rosuvastatin, a cholesterol medicine.
Because of these effects, a prescriber needs a full list of your other medicines and supplements.
pregnancyAndChildren: Asciminib is not for use in pregnancy. The label says it can cause fetal harm, based on animal studies and on how the drug works. There are no human pregnancy data to judge the real risk. People who could become pregnant are asked to confirm they are not pregnant before starting. Effective contraception is advised during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose. Breastfeeding is also advised against during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose. That is because nobody knows whether asciminib passes into breast milk or how it might affect a breastfed child. Safety and effectiveness in children have not been established. Animal findings suggest the drug may impair fertility in females. Whether that reverses is not known.
whatWeDoNotKnow: No one has human data on asciminib use in pregnancy, so the pregnancy warning rests on animal studies.
There is no information on whether asciminib passes into breast milk or affects a breastfed child.
Whether the fertility effect seen in animals reverses is unknown.
The approval for newly diagnosed CML is accelerated. It rests on response rates, and continued approval depends on a later trial confirming real clinical benefit.
Most safety numbers here come from one pooled group of 556 people in three trials. The label warns that rates from different trials cannot be compared directly.
This record leaves out dosing on purpose. Amounts differ by situation, and only your cancer team can set yours.

gaps: MedlinePlus drug monographs were not used. NLM states they are licensed from the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists. Only MedlinePlus health topic, genetics and medical test pages appear here.
NCCIH was checked and has no asciminib page. The address https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/asciminib returns 404. There is no NCCIH summary of this substance to draw on.

LiverTox is a public-domain NIDDK source and does have an asciminib page at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK597219/. Two fetch attempts returned a browser-verification page instead of content. No LiverTox claim is used here, so its statement about liver injury in asciminib users does not appear.
Several guessed FDA page addresses returned 404. One was the FDA D.I.S.C.O. burst page on the 2021 Scemblix approval. Only the two FDA approval-summary pages cited in evidence were reachable.
No reachable source states how many people with CML take asciminib in routine practice. Real-world use cannot be described.
The sources checked do not show whether asciminib improves long-term survival compared with other CML drugs. The newly diagnosed indication is still an accelerated approval.
Dosing is deliberately absent. The label records different amounts for different situations. Reporting them would read as a personal protocol, which this record does not give.
summary: Covers what asciminib is, which adults with Philadelphia chromosome-positive CML it is approved for, its trial response rates, its side effects and interactions, and the pregnancy, child and unknown-answer limits.
